summary: Recommends that routers stop forwarding directed broadcasts by default, which helps prevent attacks that use a network to flood a victim. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: A directed broadcast is one message addressed to every computer on a network. The old router rules made routers pass such messages along by default, but on the Internet backbone those messages were almost always attacks. This memo changes the default so routers block them unless an administrator switches the feature on.

subtitle: This memo flips the default so routers block directed broadcasts unless an operator turns the feature on.

tldr.problem: RFC 1812 required routers to receive and forward directed broadcasts by default, even though on the Internet backbone their use appeared to consist entirely of malicious attacks on other networks.
tldr.mechanism: The memo replaces two passages of RFC 1812 so that receiving and forwarding network-prefix-directed broadcasts are options that MUST default to blocking.
tldr.outcome: Newly deployed routers no longer add to the Smurf amplifier problem unless the operator deliberately enables the feature.

today: RFC 2644 is Best Current Practice 34 and updates RFC 1812. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Old Default and Why It Changed
sections.content:
Router Requirements (RFC 1812) specified that routers must receive and forward directed broadcasts. It also required routers to have an option to disable the feature, but said that option MUST default to permitting the receiving and forwarding.

The author notes that directed broadcasts have uses, yet on the Internet backbone their use appears to consist entirely of malicious attacks on other networks. Changing the required default would help keep new routers connected to the Internet from adding to the problems already present.
sections.plainLanguage: A directed broadcast is one message addressed to every computer on a network. The older router rules required routers to pass these messages along unless told otherwise. Because the only serious use on the Internet backbone was attacks, this memo changes the default to blocking.

sections.title: Smurf Attacks and Amplifiers
sections.content:
Damaging denial of service attacks led to the writing of RFC 2267 on Ingress Filtering. A recent trend in Smurf Attacks is to target networks that permit directed broadcasts from outside their networks. By permitting them, those systems become Smurf Amplifiers.

Ingress filtering remains the best way to limit these attacks, but restricting directed broadcasts should also receive priority. Network service providers and corporate network operators are urged to ensure their networks are not susceptible to directed broadcast packets originating outside their networks.

The memo also notes that Mobile IP (RFC 2002) had provisions for directed broadcasts in dynamic agent discovery. It is unclear whether that is useful, and the text suggests it may be worth considering removing that language.
sections.plainLanguage: A network that accepts these broadcasts from outside can be used to multiply an attacker's traffic onto a victim, and the RFC calls such a network a Smurf Amplifier. Operators are urged to close that opening, even though filtering at the source remains the best defense.

sections.title: The New Router Requirements
sections.content:
Section 4.2.2.11 (d) of RFC 1812 is replaced. A directed broadcast of the form { <Network-prefix>, -1 } MUST NOT be used as a source address. A router MAY originate such packets, and MAY have a configuration option to receive them, but that option MUST be disabled by default, so the router MUST NOT receive them unless the end user configures it.

The second paragraph of section 5.3.5.2 is replaced as well. A router MAY have options to enable receiving and forwarding network-prefix-directed broadcasts on an interface, and these options MUST default to blocking receipt and blocking forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: Under the new rules a router starts with the feature switched off. It must not receive or forward these broadcasts unless an administrator deliberately turns the option on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The purpose of the memo is security: to reduce the efficacy of certain types of denial of service attacks. The RFC lists no other security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The aim is to make some kinds of denial of service attacks less effective. The RFC mentions no other security effects.
